claim: The NuRD complex is a multi-protein transcriptional corepressor that couples histone deacetylase and ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling activities.
source: The NuRD complex is a multi-protein transcriptional corepressor that couples histone deacetylase and ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling activities.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the NuRD complex that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The NuRD complex regulates the higher-order structure of chromatin.
source: The complex regulates the higher-order structure of chromatin, and has important roles in the regulation of gene expression, DNA damage repair and cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about NuRD complex function.

claim: The NuRD complex has important roles in the regulation of gene expression, DNA damage repair and cell differentiation.
source: The complex regulates the higher-order structure of chromatin, and has important roles in the regulation of gene expression, DNA damage repair and cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about NuRD complex function.

claim: HDACs 1 and 2 are recruited by the MTA1 corepressor to form the catalytic core of the complex.
source: HDACs 1 and 2 are recruited by the MTA1 corepressor to form the catalytic core of the complex.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about NuRD complex assembly.

claim: The histone chaperone protein RBBP4 has previously been shown to bind to the carboxy-terminal tail of MTA1.
source: The histone chaperone protein RBBP4, has previously been shown to bind to the carboxy-terminal tail of MTA1.
evidence: This statement references prior published work on RBBP4-MTA1 interaction.

claim: MTA1 recruits a second copy of RBBP4.
source: We show that MTA1 recruits a second copy of RBBP4.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including MALS and crystallography.

claim: The crystal structure reveals an extensive interface between MTA1 and RBBP4.
source: The crystal structure reveals an extensive interface between MTA1 and RBBP4.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An EM structure, supported by SAXS and crosslinking, reveals the architecture of the dimeric HDAC1:MTA1:RBBP4 assembly which forms the core of the NuRD complex.
source: An EM structure, supported by SAXS and crosslinking, reveals the architecture of the dimeric HDAC1:MTA1:RBBP4 assembly which forms the core of the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental techniques (EM, SAXS, crosslinking) presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the NuRD complex, RBBP4 mediates interaction with histone H3 tails, but not histone H4.
source: We find evidence that in this complex RBBP4 mediates interaction with histone H3 tails, but not histone H4, suggesting a mechanism for recruitment of the NuRD complex to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by peptide array binding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NuRD complex is one of at least five corepressor complexes that recruits and activates class I histone deacetylase (HDACs) enzymes.
source: The nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex is one of at least five corepressor complexes that recruits and activates class I histone deacetylase (HDACs) enzymes and directs their activity to chromatin (Bantscheff et al., 2011; Guenther et al., 2000; Humphrey et al., 2001; Itoh et al., 2015; Kelly and Cowley, 2013; Laherty et al., 1997; Oberoi et al., 2011; Vermaak et al., 1999; Watson et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2000; Xue et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The NuRD complex plays a major role in the regulation of gene expression as well as being involved in chromatin organization, DNA damage repair, and genomic stability.
source: The NuRD complex plays a major role in the regulation of gene expression as well as being involved in chromatin organization, DNA damage repair, and genomic stability (Denslow and Wade, 2007; Lai and Wade, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NuRD complex is composed of six proteins, each with several isoforms: HDAC1/2, MTA1/2/3, RBBP4/7, P66α/β, MBD2/3, and CHD3/4.
source: The NuRD complex is composed of six proteins, each with several isoforms: HDAC1/2, MTA1/2/3, RBBP4/7, P66α/β, MBD2/3, and CHD3/4 (Allen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The NuRD complex exhibits dual enzymatic functionality through its HDAC (protein deacetylation) and ATPase (chromatin remodelling) domains.
source: The complex is special in its ability to exhibit dual enzymatic functionality through its HDAC (protein deacetylation) and ATPase (chromatin remodelling) domains.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about NuRD complex function.

claim: Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) are important regulators of transcription that are involved in silencing genes and/or priming them for successive rounds of transcription.
source: Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) are important regulators of transcription that are involved in silencing genes and/or priming them for successive rounds of transcription (Micelli and Rastelli, 2015; Verdin and Ott, 2014; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HDACs act by removing the acetyl groups from modified lysine residues on histone tails and other non-histone proteins.
source: HDACs act by removing the acetyl groups from modified lysine residues on histone tails and other non-histone proteins.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about HDAC enzymatic function.

claim: HDACs have been shown to be overexpressed in various cancer tissues.
source: These enzymes have been shown to be overexpressed in various cancer tissues and several inhibitors against these enzymes are currently used in the clinic as anti-cancer therapeutics (Falkenberg and Johnstone, 2014; Marks and Xu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several HDAC inhibitors are currently used in the clinic as anti-cancer therapeutics.
source: These enzymes have been shown to be overexpressed in various cancer tissues and several inhibitors against these enzymes are currently used in the clinic as anti-cancer therapeutics (Falkenberg and Johnstone, 2014; Marks and Xu, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Metastasis-associated protein 1 (MTA1) and its closely related homologues MTA2 and 3 are up-regulated in various cancer tissues.
source: Metastasis-associated protein 1 (MTA1) (and its closely related homologues MTA2 and 3) are up-regulated in various cancer tissues (Fujita et al., 2003; Li et al., 2012; Sen et al., 2014; Toh et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MTA proteins serve as scaffold proteins for the assembly of the NuRD complex.
source: They serve as scaffold proteins for the assembly of the NuRD complex.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about MTA protein function.

claim: The amino-terminal region of MTA proteins contains four established domains: an amino-terminal BAH domain, followed by ELM2 and SANT domains, and a GATA-like zinc finger domain towards the centre of the protein.
source: The amino-terminal region contains four established domains: an amino-terminal BAH domain, followed by ELM2 and SANT domains, and a GATA-like zinc finger domain towards the centre of the protein (Manavathi and Kumar, 2007; Millard et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ELM2 domain has been shown by X-ray crystallography to mediate dimerization of the complex.
source: The ELM2 domain has been shown by X-ray crystallography to mediate dimerization of the complex and, in conjunction with the SANT domain, recruits HDAC1 & 2 (Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior crystallographic work.

claim: The ELM2 domain, in conjunction with the SANT domain, recruits HDAC1 & 2.
source: The ELM2 domain has been shown by X-ray crystallography to mediate dimerization of the complex and, in conjunction with the SANT domain, recruits HDAC1 & 2 (Millard et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior crystallographic work.

claim: A short helix at the very carboxy-terminus of MTA1 and MTA2 has been shown to mediate interaction with RBBP4/7.
source: The exception is at the very carboxy-terminus of MTA1 and MTA2 where a short helix has been shown to mediate interaction with RBBP4/7 (Alqarni et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A binding site for CHD4 has been identified in the carboxy-terminal region of MTA proteins, but has not been structurally characterised.
source: A binding site for CHD4 has also been identified in this region, but has not been structurally characterised (Nair et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are homologous (92% identical) histone binding proteins.
source: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are homologous (92% identical) histone binding proteins (also known as RbAp48 and RbAp46) that have been shown to be core components of the NuRD complex.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about RBBP4/7 sequence similarity.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 have been shown to be core components of the NuRD complex.
source: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are homologous (92% identical) histone binding proteins (also known as RbAp48 and RbAp46) that have been shown to be core components of the NuRD complex.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about NuRD complex composition.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are present in multiple complexes including other class I HDAC corepressors such as the Sin3A and PRC2 complexes.
source: These proteins are unusual in that they are present in multiple complexes including other class I HDAC corepressors such as the Sin3A and PRC2 complexes (Ciferri et al., 2012; Kuzmichev, 2002; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RBBP4, along with sNASP and Asf1 forms a multi chaperone complex whose function is to maintain a supply of newly synthesized histone H3 and H4 proteins under replicative stress.
source: RBBP4, along with sNASP and Asf1 forms a multi chaperone complex whose function is to maintain a supply of newly synthesized histone H3 and H4 proteins under replicative stress (Groth et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RBBP4 has been found to be a subunit of the chromatin-assembly factor-1 (CAF-1) complex whose function is to initiate nucleosome assembly by assembling histones H3 and H4 onto newly synthesized DNA.
source: RBBP4 has also been found to be a subunit of the chromatin-assembly factor-1 (CAF-1) complex whose function is to initiate nucleosome assembly by assembling histones H3 and H4 onto newly synthesized DNA (Parthun et al., 1996; Verreault et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RBBP7 has been found to be an essential subunit of the HAT1 histone-acetyltransferase complex, which acetylates newly synthesized histone proteins.
source: In addition, RBBP7 has been found to be an essential subunit of the HAT1 histone-acetyltransferase complex, which acetylates newly synthesized histone proteins (Verreault et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 have been shown to interact directly with histone H3 and H4 tails through two distinct binding sites.
source: RBBP4 and RBBP7 have been shown to interact directly with histone H3 and H4 tails through two distinct binding sites and therefore have the potential to act as chromatin recruitment modules (Murzina et al., 2008; Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011; Song et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 have the potential to act as chromatin recruitment modules.
source: RBBP4 and RBBP7 have been shown to interact directly with histone H3 and H4 tails through two distinct binding sites and therefore have the potential to act as chromatin recruitment modules (Murzina et al., 2008; Nowak et al., 2011; Schmitges et al., 2011; Song et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and logical inference from the histone binding capability.

claim: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are WD40 domain proteins with a characteristic seven bladed β-propeller structure.
source: RBBP4 and RBBP7 are WD40 domain proteins with a characteristic seven bladed β-propeller structure (Xu and Min, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RBBP4/7 interacts with histone H3 through a binding site on the 'top' face of the protein.
source: RBBP4/7 interacts with histone H3 through a binding site on the 'top' face of the protein (Schmitges et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The RBBP4/7 WD40 domain has an amino-terminal helix of 30 residues that forms an extension to the β-propeller domain.
source: A particular feature of the RBBP4/7 WD40 domain is an amino-terminal helix of 30 residues that forms an extension to the β-propeller domain.
evidence: This statement is based on established structural knowledge about RBBP4/7.

claim: A groove formed adjacent to the amino-terminal helix of RBBP4/7 mediates interaction with the amino-terminus of histone H4.
source: A groove that is formed adjacent to this helix mediates interaction with the amino-terminus of histone H4 (Murzina et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The extreme carboxy-terminus of MTA1 (residues 671–690) has been shown to interact with RBBP4/7 in the groove adjacent to the amino-terminal helix, making very similar contacts to those made by histone H4.
source: Interestingly, the extreme carboxy-terminus of MTA1 (residues 671–690) has been shown to interact with RBBP4/7 in this groove, making very similar contacts to those made by histone H4 (Alqarni et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A second RBBP4 recruitment site has been identified within MTA1 that is positioned near the centre of the corepressor.
source: In this study, we have identified a second RBBP4 recruitment site within MTA1 that is positioned near the centre of the corepressor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The second RBBP4 recruitment site shows some sequence homology to the previously characterised carboxy-terminal recruitment site, but is considerably more extensive.
source: This site shows some sequence homology to the previously characterised carboxy-terminal recruitment site, but is considerably more extensive.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both RBBP4 recruitment sites within the MTA1 monomer are capable of independently recruiting RBBP4 proteins.
source: We show that both sites within the MTA1 monomer are capable of independently recruiting RBBP4 proteins such that the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer recruits four molecules of RBBP4 to the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including MALS and binding studies.

claim: The HDAC1:MTA1 dimer recruits four molecules of RBBP4 to the NuRD complex.
source: We show that both sites within the MTA1 monomer are capable of independently recruiting RBBP4 proteins such that the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer recruits four molecules of RBBP4 to the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including MALS and stoichiometry analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of the central recruitment site reveals an extensive interface that requires some structural rearrangement within RBBP4.
source: The crystal structure of this central recruitment site reveals an extensive interface that requires some structural rearrangement within RBBP4.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RBBP4 proteins are tethered to the HDAC1 dimer by MTA1 forming an elongated zig-zag conformation.
source: RBBP4 proteins are tethered to the HDAC1 dimer by MTA1 forming an elongated zig-zag conformation.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS and EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When in complex with MTA1, RBBP4 is able to interact with histone H3, but not histone H4.
source: We show that when in complex with MTA1, RBBP4 is able to interact with histone H3, but not histone H4 suggesting a mechanism for recruitment of the NuRD complex to chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by peptide array binding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An endogenous protein of c. 50kDa co-purified with HDAC1:MTA1 complexes expressed in mammalian cells.
source: During purifications of various HDAC1:MTA1 complexes expressed in mammalian cells, we observed an endogenous protein of c. 50kDa co-purifying with these complexes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Peptide mass spectrometry identified the c. 50kDa co-purifying protein as being the WD40 protein RBBP4 and/or RBBP7.
source: Peptide mass spectrometry identified this protein as being the WD40 protein RBBP4 and/or RBBP7.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from the study.

claim: RBBP4/7 was recruited to MTA1 constructs that lacked the well-characterised carboxy-terminal interaction domain.
source: However, we were intrigued to find that RBBP4/7 was recruited to constructs that lacked this well-characterised interaction domain.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Previous findings indicated that RBBP4/7 may interact with a region containing the MTA1 zinc finger domain and adjacent sequences.
source: This appears to fit with previous findings that indicated that RBBP4/7 may interact with a region containing the MTA1 zinc finger domain and adjacent sequences (Roche et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The MTA1-B construct spanning residues 162–546 pulls down a stoichiometric 1:1 ratio of HDAC1:RBBP4/7.
source: Importantly, the MTA1-B construct spanning residues 162–546 appears to pull down a stoichiometric 1:1 ratio of HDAC1:RBBP4/7 suggesting that this region is sufficient to form a bona fide interface with RBBP4/7.
evidence: This is supported by gel densitometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MTA1 construct spanning residues 162–715 (MTA1-C) pulls down a supra-stoichiometric ratio of 1:1.5 of HDAC1:RBBP4/7.
source: Interesting a construct spanning residues 162–715 (MTA1-C) pulls down a supra-stoichiometric ratio of 1:1.5 of HDAC1:RBBP4/7.
evidence: This is supported by gel densitometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MTA1-D:RBBP4 complex (MTA1 residues 390–715) has a molecular weight of 130 kDa as determined by MALS.
source: The longer fragment of MTA1-D (residues 390–715) in complex with RBBP4 was shown to have a molecular weight of 130 kDa (Figures 1d and 1f; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MALS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The molecular weight of 130 kDa for the MTA1-D:RBBP4 complex closely fits with the predicted molecular weight (131 kDa) of a 1:2 stoichiometry of one MTA1 fragment bound to two RBBP4 proteins.
source: This closely fits with the predicted molecular weight (131 kDa) of a 1:2 stoichiometry of one MTA1 fragment bound to two RBBP4 proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MALS data and theoretical molecular weight calculation.

claim: The MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex (MTA1 residues 464–546) has a molecular weight of 54 kDa as determined by MALS.
source: The shorter MTA1-R1 fragment (residues 464–546) in complex with RBBP4 was determined to have a molecular weight of 54 kDa which is close to the predicted molecular weight of 58 kDa for the 1:1 complex (Figures 1e and 1g; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MALS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Two RBBP4 proteins are recruited by MTA1 to the NuRD complex.
source: It is clear that these experiments support a model in which two RBBP4 proteins are recruited by MTA1 to the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The interface between MTA1-R1 and RBBP4 is extensive with a buried surface area of 2,837 Å2.
source: The interface between MTA1-R1 and RBBP4 is extensive with a buried surface area of 2,837 Å2 (Figures 2a and 2b, Table 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: MTA1 interacts on the side of the WD40 beta-propeller domain making interactions in three adjacent grooves.
source: MTA1 interacts on the side of the WD40 beta-propeller domain making interactions in three adjacent grooves.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The residues involved in all three interaction regions between MTA1-R1 and RBBP4 are conserved in both MTA2 and MTA3.
source: The residues involved in all three interaction regions are conserved in both MTA2 and MTA3 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The 5G-loop in RBBP4 adopts an ordered structure on MTA1 binding.
source: The 5G-loop adopts an ordered structure on MTA1 binding such that several non-polar residues form an additional interface with MTA1.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The HDAC1:MTA1 complex is dimeric, containing two copies of each protein.
source: Multi-Angle-Light-Scattering (MALS) confirmed that, as expected from the crystal structure, the HDAC1:MTA1 complex is dimeric, containing two copies of each protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MALS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The theoretical scattering profile calculated from the crystal structure of HDAC1:MTA1 was in good agreement with the experimental SAXS data with a χ2 function of 1.54.
source: A theoretical scattering profile was calculated from the crystal structure of HDAC1:MTA1 (Millard et al., 2013) and this was in good agreement with the experimental data with a χ2 function of 1.54.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer was a convincing fit to the averaged ab initio molecular envelope generated from the SAXS curve.
source: Furthermore, the crystal structure of the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer was a convincing fit to the averaged ab initio molecular envelope generated from the SAXS curve (Figures 3a, 3b and 3c).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data and modeling shown in Figure 3.

claim: MALS analysis of the MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex showed that this ensemble is dimeric, with the experimental mass of 300 kDa closely matching the theoretical mass (294 kDa).
source: MALS analysis of the MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex showed that this ensemble is also dimeric, with the experimental mass of 300 kDa closely matching the theoretical mass (294 kDa) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MALS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ab initio molecular envelope generated from the SAXS curve suggests that the core NuRD complex has an elongated architecture.
source: The ab initio molecular envelope generated from the SAXS curve in the lowest symmetry mode (P1) suggests that the core NuRD complex has an elongated architecture (Figures 3d,e and f).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The SAXS envelope has an approximate two-fold symmetry consistent with a dimeric complex.
source: Although no symmetry was imposed, the envelope has an approximate two-fold symmetry consistent with a dimeric complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the SAXS data analysis.

claim: Crosslinking data indicated that one face of HDAC1 could readily form crosslinks with one face of RBBP4.
source: Our crosslinking data indicated that one face of HDAC1 could readily form crosslinks with one face of RBBP4, suggesting a particular relative orientation of the two proteins in the core complex.
evidence: This is supported by chemical crosslinking data.

claim: A theoretical scattering profile calculated from the docked model of the MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex showed reasonable agreement with the experimental SAXS data with a χ2 function of 2.16.
source: A theoretical scattering profile was calculated from the docked model of the MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex. This showed reasonable agreement with the experimental data with a χ2 function of 2.16.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data analysis.

claim: The EM structure of the core NuRD complex was determined to 19 Å resolution using the FSC criterion with a cutoff of 0.143.
source: A 30 Å filtered model was then generated, based on the new position of RBBP4, and refined further to produce a 19 Å EM structure using the FSC criterion with a cutoff of 0.143 (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The EM envelope showed that RBBP4 and HDAC1 form a closer association than predicted in the SAXS model.
source: The resulting EM envelope showed that RBBP4 and HDAC1 form a closer association than predicted in the SAXS model.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing EM and SAXS models.

claim: In the EM structure, the RBBP4 domains are tipped by 30° such that they are approximately parallel to each other and propagate the symmetry of the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer.
source: In their new position the RBBP4 domains are tipped by 30° such that they are approximately parallel to each other and propagate the symmetry of the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer.
evidence: This is an observation from the EM structure.

claim: The active sites of both HDACs are on the convex side of the complex and are exposed to enable substrate binding.
source: The active sites of both HDACs are on the convex side of the complex and are exposed to enable substrate binding.
evidence: This is an observation from the EM structure.

claim: A stretch of c.35 residues is highly similar between the R1 and R2 recruitment regions of MTA1.
source: Sequence alignment show that a stretch of c.35 residues is highly similar between the two recruitment regions (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The path of the mainchain from P492 to I503 in the R1 domain is essentially identical to the equivalent region of the R2 domain when bound to RBBP4.
source: Comparison of this structure with that of the equivalent region of the R1 domain (region B in the description above) shows a highly similar mode of binding to RBBP4 (Figure 5b). Indeed, the path of the mainchain from P492 to I503 is essentially identical.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The sidechains A495, A496 and R497 in helix H2 and P499, Y500, P502 and I503 in the PYxPI loop mediate key interactions with RBBP4 and are identical in the R2 domain.
source: The sidechains A495, A496 and R497 in helix H2 and P499, Y500, P502 and I503 in the PYxPI loop mediate key interactions with RBBP4 and are identical in the R2 domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural and sequence analysis.

claim: The interface between RBBP4 and the R2 domain is likely to be rather more extensive than was observed in the previously reported crystal structure.
source: The sequence alignment also indicates that the 15 residues preceding helix 2 in the R2 domain have significant sequence similarity to the R1 domain suggesting that the interface between RBBP4 and the R2 domain is likely to be rather more extensive than was observed in the previously reported crystal structure (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The surface of RBBP4 that mediates interactions with helix H2 of the R1 and R2 domains of MTA1 has also been shown to mediate interactions with the amino-terminal region of histone H4.
source: The surface of RBBP4 that mediates interactions with helix H2 of the R1 and R2 domains of MTA1 has also been shown to mediate interactions with the amino-terminal region of histone H4.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: There is considerable sequence similarity between the MTA1-R1 and -R2 domains and histone H4.
source: Sequence alignment of the MTA1-R1 and -R2 domains with histone H4 shows that there is considerable sequence similarity between these proteins.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The structure of histone H4 (residues 27–41) in complex with RBBP4 shows a similar mode of binding to the structure of the bound MTA1-R1 and -R2 domains.
source: The structure of histone H4 (residues 27–41) in complex with RBBP4 shows a similar mode of binding to the structure of the bound MTA1-R1 and -R2 domains (Figure 5c) (Murzina et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5c and citation to prior work.

claim: All three proteins (MTA1-R1, MTA1-R2, and histone H4) bind in the same groove on RBBP4 and make similar sidechain contacts with an Alanine-Arginine dipeptide making identical contacts in all three structures.
source: All three proteins bind in the same groove and make similar sidechain contacts with an Alanine-Arginine dipeptide making identical contacts in all three structures (Figures 5b and 5c).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figures 5b and 5c.

claim: The extensive interface between RBBP4 and the R1 domain of MTA1 occludes the binding site for histone H4.
source: However, given that the extensive interface between RBBP4 and the R1 domain of MTA1 (and by inference the R2 domain) occludes the binding site for histone H4, we would predict that RBBP4 is no longer able to bind histone H4 in the NuRD complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The histone H3 interaction site on RBBP4 is exposed in both the MTA1:RBBP4 binary complex and in the dimeric MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex.
source: However, the histone H3 interaction on RBBP4 is exposed in both the MTA1:RBBP4 binary complex and in the dimeric MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: RBBP4 is likely to play a role in recruiting the NuRD complex to histone H3 tails, but not to histone H4.
source: This implies that RBBP4 is likely to play a role in recruiting the NuRD complex to histone H3 tails, but not to histone H4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing H3 binding site is exposed while H4 binding site is occluded.

claim: Both RBBP4 and the MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex showed an identical pattern of binding to histone H3 peptides.
source: As predicted, we observed that both RBBP4 and the MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex showed an identical pattern of binding to histone H3 peptides.
evidence: This is supported by peptide array binding data.

claim: Free RBBP4 bound multiple histone H4 tails.
source: The free RBBP4 bound multiple histone H4 tails.
evidence: This is supported by peptide array binding data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex showed only binding to two histone H4 peptides and this was not reproduced in the duplicate arrays.
source: In contrast, the MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex showed only binding to two histone H4 peptides and this was not reproduced in the duplicate arrays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by peptide array binding data shown in Figure 6.

claim: When bound to MTA1, RBBP4 binds to histone H3 and not histone H4.
source: Taken together this suggests that when bound to MTA1, RBBP4 binds to histone H3 and not histone H4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the peptide array binding data.

claim: The core NuRD complex forms an elongated zig-zag structure centred around the HDAC1:MTA1 dimerization domain, with RBBP4 'lobes' symmetrically bound to the dimer.
source: This core complex forms an elongated zig-zag structure as visualised by SAXS and EM, centred around the HDAC1:MTA1 dimerization domain, with RBBP4 'lobes' symmetrically bound to the dimer.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS and EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A central section of MTA1 directly recruits RBBP4/7 and brings this subunit into close proximity to HDAC1/2.
source: We have established that a central section of MTA1 directly recruits RBBP4/7 and brings this subunit into close proximity to HDAC1/2.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each MTA1 protein recruits two RBBP4/7 molecules to the NuRD complex through the R1 and R2 interaction domains.
source: We have shown that each MTA1 protein recruits two RBBP4/7 molcules to the NuRD complex through the R1 and R2 interaction domains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including MALS and stoichiometry analysis.

claim: Since MTA1 is a dimer in the complex, the NuRD complex contains four copies of the RBBP4/7 proteins.
source: Since MTA1 is itself a dimer in the complex (Millard et al., 2013) this means that the NuRD complex contains four copies of the RBBP4/7 proteins, which we have confirmed experimentally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dimeric nature of MTA1 and the experimental data showing two RBBP4 per MTA1.

claim: Recognisable R1 and R2 interaction domains are present in MTA1 and 2 proteins from fly to man suggesting that the stoichiometry of the NuRD complex is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Recognisable R1 and R2 interaction domains are present in MTA1 and 2 proteins from fly to man suggesting that the stoichiometry of the NuRD complex is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: A previous study using label-free mass spectrometry reported a 1:2 MTA1:RBBP4/7 stoichiometry.
source: Our findings fit partially with a previous study of the NuRD complex using label-free mass spectrometry. In this study they also report a 1:2 MTA1:RBBP4/7 stoichiometry, but in contrast to our previous crystal structure of the MTA1:HDAC1 complex, they find a 1:3 HDAC:MTA stoichiometry (Smits et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A previous study using label-free mass spectrometry found a 1:3 HDAC:MTA stoichiometry.
source: Our findings fit partially with a previous study of the NuRD complex using label-free mass spectrometry. evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Alqarni et al. used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to compare the affinity of interaction of the helical region of the R2 domain from MTA1 (656–686) with that of histone H4.
source: Alqarni et al. used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to compare the affinity of interaction of the helical region of the R2 domain from MTA1 (656–686) with that of histone H4, which they observed bound in the same groove of RBBP4.
evidence: This statement references prior published work.

claim: The similarity in affinity between MTA1-R2 and histone H4 for RBBP4 led to the suggestion that there may be competition between MTA1 and histone H4 for binding to RBBP4.
source: The similarity in affinity led them to suggest that there may be competition between MTA1 and histone H4 for binding to RBBP4 (Alqarni et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references a suggestion from prior published work.

claim: There is likely to be a more extensive interface between MTA1-R2 and RBBP4 with an additional helix and beta-strand contributing to the interaction.
source: Our findings suggest that there is likely to be a more extensive interface between MTA1-R2 and RBBP4 with an additional helix and beta-strand contributing to the interaction.

source: Given this extended interface we suggest that histone H4 is unlikely to be able to compete with either MTA1-R1 or R2 for binding to RBBP4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing the extensive interface.

claim: The MTA1-R1:RBBP4 complex appeared highly stable since the resin-bound complex could be washed with 2 M NaCl and 5% triton-X-100 without significant dissociation.

source: Taken together our data suggest that once bound to MTA1, the two RBBP4 molcules would remain permanently assembled as a complex.

source: Such a model of recruitment to histone H3 is consistent with the architecture of the MTA1:HDAC1:RBBP4 complex since the orientation of RBBP4 relative to the HDAC1:MTA1 dimer means that the histone H3 binding surface of RBBP4 is exposed, albeit close to the interface between HDAC1 and RBBP4, and therefore able to bind the tail of histone H3.

source: Our structural data suggest that the residues important for mediating interaction with MTA1 are 100% identical and therefore we would expect both RBBP4 and RBBP7 to be associated with the NuRD complex depending upon relative abundance.
